US-China summit delivers 'modest but practical' outcomes: Citi
The big US investment bank Citi says the just concluded US-China summit delivered "modest but practical" outcomes.

Those outcomes included a two-month trade "truce" extension, a $US30 billion Board of Trade tariff reduction, a new AI dialogue and an agreement for further meetings at APEC in Shenzhen (Nov 18–19) and the G20 in Miami (Dec 14–15).

Citi's chief China economist, Xiangrong Yu, said the meeting delivered on optics with the prospect of further meetings this year "would see an unprecedented four Trump-Xi meetings, helping lower near-term risk of any breakdown in relations".

"The renewed stability commitment would perhaps ease risks such as new restrictions on Chinese AI infrastructure products and open-weight models as well as large-scale US arms sales to Taiwan within this year," Yu said.
The two sides agreed to communicate on AI incidents.

"With the coordination mechanisms in place, neither Washington nor Beijing appears inclined to slow AI development — rather, the dialogue offers a channel to address mutual concerns without resorting to more confrontational measures such as expanded export controls," Yu wrote in a research note over the weekend.
He said the summit didn't produce major economic outcomes beyond the two-month extension of the trade "truce."
"We are not concerned by the short extension window, as it can be pushed further at the next Trump-Xi meeting around APEC or the G20—and a broader deal is not out of the question."
Both sides confirmed $US30 billion in goods under the Board of Trade for reciprocal tariff cuts.

The White House fact sheet detailed US export categories—agricultural goods, fish & seafood, logs & wood products, cosmetics, and medical devices—alongside Chinese export categories including small appliances, toys, holiday decorations, and children's car seats.
Separately, the fact sheet flagged China's coal imports of 10mn tons in 2027-28.
"Following the summit, we see a lower chance of a breakdown in US-China relations within the year, averting the kind of tariff-driven volatility that markets experienced last year," Yu added.
US, China agree to tariff cuts, AI dialogue
The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on $US30 billion of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.
The tariff reductions would apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood and cosmetics, as well as US imports including small appliances, toys, decorations, a White House statement said.
"The two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.

The three-day summit between Xi and President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.
The two sides also agreed to set up a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.

On artificial intelligence, the two sides agreed to hold a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, and to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.

It's a busy week in the economic diary, although the RBA rates decision (Tuesday) will tend to overshadow everything locally.
A full 25 bps rate hike has been priced in by the market. Most market economists — and the big four retail banks — agree.
Certainly, a barrage of RBA-speak in recent weeks has pointed to a hike, and anything else would be a major surprise.

The Minutes of the August meeting stated that Board members thought it may be appropriate to tighten policy "pre-emptively" if risks to the inflation forecast were judged to be "significantly skewed to the upside". As Societe Generale pointed out in a note over the weekend, this is now playing out.

"RBA staff also argued a 'pre-emptive approach' to tightening is needed when the economy is subject to capacity constraints and adverse supply shocks, and this is currently the case." Societe Generale said.
September CPI inflation is released the day after (Wednesday).
While there has been much furrowing of brows and cliched hectoring of the RBA about putting the cart-before-the-horse, it doesn't really matter.

Inflation is very unlikely to suddenly disappear, nor is the RBA boardroom suddenly going resemble a cooing dovecote. The hawkish sentiment is aimed at getting ahead of the problem, rather than reacting to it.

If anything, the threat is inflation will come in even hotter than the RBA hoped for — with the consensus forecast showing trimmed mean inflation at 3.6%, and headline inflation lifting from 3.5% to perhaps 4%.
We'll get important updates on the housing market.
Building approvals (Wednesday) are always volatile. They fell marginally in July, and the consensus, without great conviction, is they will fall again.
Depending on your view of things, home prices are expected to fall again nationally/housing affordability is expected to improve.

Australia's trade surplus has been narrowing in recent months, but an increase in iron ore and coal shipments and prices may well see the surplus widen again beyond $2 billion in August. Once again, volatile gold exports make tipping it accurately a mug's game.
Overseas, the main interest will be US PCE inflation and jobs data.

The Fed's preferred measure of inflation, Personal Consumption Expenditure (Wed) is likely to have taken another step up to 0.4% month-on-month in August, mainly thanks to higher fuel prices. It gained 0.2% in July.
Nonfarm payrolls (Friday) are likely to show around 80-thousand new jobs were created in the US in September, which would be in line with the recent trend. Unemployment is likely t hold at 4.1%.
Key Event
Wall Street gains while ASX lacks direction
The three key Wall Street indices made solid gains on Friday to close a volatile week.
• Dow: +%
• Nasdaq: +0.4%
Overall, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq gained 1.2% and 2% respectively for the week.
Eurozone shares also finished positively (+0.5%) to pick up 0.8% for the week.
However, the ASX, ahead of this week's likely RBA rate rise, remained under pressure, clocking the fourth successive losing week, down 0.8%.
Futures trading on the ASX shows the bleeding may have been cauterised, at least briefly, but the pulse is weak.
A gain of just 0.03%, or 3 points, was priced in when trading closed on Saturday morning.
Wall Street's gain was driven by an almost 4% jump in Microsoft shares after announcing its AI tool Copilot had new capabilities.
Chipmaker Qualcom gained 4% as well, while Akamai Technologies rallied 3.2% after an $US11.6 billion cloud services deal with AI leader Anthropic.
The deal, another one of those circular trades in vogue in the AI sector, includes a warrant that could give Anthropic up to 5% of Akamai.

"That's a positive from the standpoint that people are still investing, deals are still being done," Globalt Investments portfolio manager Thomas Martin, said without much enthusiasm."It's another circular deal, so OK … but Akamai stock is up."

"It's another circular deal, so OK … but Akamai stock is up."

Meta Platforms dipped 3.3% after the social media company's stock soared about 13% this week amid a strong reception to its Muse AI agent, which analysts say could benefit tech infrastructure stocks, while challenging banks, online shopping platforms and other consumer businesses.
Interestingly, the big earnings upgrades among the AI titans now sees the S&P 500 trading at its lowest level (19 times expected earnings) since 2023.

NAB's head of FX Strategy Ray Attrill said lower oil prices on Friday, on ongoing hopes for a phased deal that would see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lift its blockade of Iranian ports, supported stocks and brought Treasuries off Friday morning's new cycle highs.

"In equity markets the S&P500 and NASDAQ both gained 0.5% Friday for weekly gains of 1.2% and 2.1% respectively, eye opening in the context of the rise in bond yields but perhaps less so in as much as the US economy, and the outlook for corporate profits, is showing no ill-effects from the rise in yields to date."
Key global oil benchmarks Brent crude and WTI crude future both fell around $US2 a barrel. However, Brent crude futures are still trading well above $US100/barrel.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note hit a fresh 19-year high and was last up 3.4 basis points at 5.196%.

"In bond markets, (there was) a little relief Friday from the intense mid-week sell off in Treasuries — and bond globally — aided by the small pull back in oil prices. 2 and 5 year Treasury yields finished Friday down 6.5bps on the day for weekly gains of 11.5 and 14bps, respectively," Mr. Attrill said.
Traders see a 66% chance of the Federal Reserve increasing interest rates by at least 25 basis points in October, up from around 50% earlier this week, the CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed.
However, the Greenback still dipped on Friday with the Aussie dollar making a marginal gain to remain above 70 US cents.

Good morning
Good morning and welcome to another day on the ABC markets and finance blog.
Stephen Letts from ABC business team limbering up for a blow-by-blow coverage of the day's events, where every post is hopefully a winner, but none should be construed as financial advice.
Wall Street closed the week higher, spurred on by some solid gains from Microsoft and chip makers.
The ASX looks very much a line ball decision between a gain and another loss today.
When trading closed on Saturday morning, ASX 200 futures pointed to the most marginal (well, third most marginal) gain of 0.03%, or three points.
Given the ASX has notched four weeks in retreat, we'll take any gain we can at the moment.
It's a quiet day on the data front ahead of tomorrow's RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting.
Anyway, the game's afoot, so let's get blogging.
